claim: Protein UFMylation downstream of the E1 enzyme UBA5 plays essential roles in development and endoplasmic reticulum stress.
source: Protein UFMylation downstream of the E1 enzyme UBA5 plays essential roles in development and endoplasmic reticulum stress.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations throughout the manuscript regarding UFMylation's role in development and ER stress.

claim: Variants in the UBA5 gene are associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 44 (DEE44), an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by early-onset encephalopathy, movement abnormalities, global developmental delay, intellectual disability, and seizures.
source: Variants in the UBA5 gene are associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 44 (DEE44), an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by early-onset encephalopathy, movement abnormalities, global developmental delay, intellectual disability, and seizures.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to clinical reports throughout the manuscript.

claim: DEE44 is caused by at least 12 different missense variants described as loss of function (LoF).
source: DEE44 is caused by at least 12 different missense variants described as loss of function (LoF), but the relationships between genotypes and molecular or clinical phenotypes remain to be established.
evidence: This is supported by the summary of reported cases in Table 1 and references to prior literature.

claim: There is a strong correlation between in vivo and in vitro phenotypes of UBA5 variants.
source: Importantly, there is a strong correlation between in vivo and in vitro phenotypes, establishing a classification of LoF variants into mild, intermediate, and severe allelic strengths.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of fly phenotypic data (Figure 4, Table 3) with biochemical assay results (Figures 6-7, Table 4).

claim: Biallelic UBA5 variants cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 44 (DEE44, OMIM: #617132) in most reported cases.
source: In most reported cases, biallelic UBA5 variants cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 44 (DEE44, OMIM: #617132).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple clinical reports (Colin et al., 2016; Muona et al., 2016).

claim: DEE44 is characterized by early-onset encephalopathy, movement abnormalities, global developmental delay, and intellectual disability.
source: The disease is characterized by early-onset encephalopathy, movement abnormalities, global developmental delay, and intellectual disability.
evidence: This is supported by clinical descriptions in cited literature.

claim: Many individuals with DEE44 also have seizures, failure to thrive, and microcephaly.
source: Many individuals also have seizures, failure to thrive, and microcephaly.
evidence: This is supported by clinical reports cited in the manuscript (Colin et al., 2016; Muona et al., 2016).

claim: Delayed myelination, thinning of the corpus callosum, and white matter hyperintensities have been documented with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in DEE44 patients.
source: Delayed myelination, thinning of the corpus callosum, and white matter hyperintensities have also been documented with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Colin et al., 2016; Muona et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical imaging studies.

claim: Biallelic UBA5 has been associated with spinocerebellar ataxia 24 (OMIM: #617133), which is characterized by a childhood-onset gait and limb ataxia.
source: Biallelic UBA5 has also been associated with spinocerebellar ataxia 24 (OMIM: #617133), which is characterized by a childhood-onset gait and limb ataxia (Duan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duan et al., 2016.

claim: A rare homozygous missense variant in UBA5 has been reported to segregate with severe congenital neuropathy.
source: Another family has been reported with a rare homozygous missense variant in UBA5 that segregates with severe congenital neuropathy (Cabrera-Serrano et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cabrera-Serrano et al., 2020.

claim: UBA5 is a key component in UFMylation, a post-translational modification pathway mediated by ubiquitin fold modifier 1 (UFM1).
source: UBA5 is a key component in UFMylation, a post-translational modification pathway mediated by a ubiquitin-like protein (UBL) ubiquitin fold modifier 1 (UFM1) (Millrine et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Millrine et al., 2023.

claim: UFMylation is conserved in metazoans and plants.
source: UFMylation is conserved in metazoans and plants (Figure 1A; Millrine et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Millrine et al., 2023 and Figure 1A showing the pathway.

claim: UFM1 is first proteolytically processed by a UFM1-specific peptidase 1/2 (UFSP1/2) to expose a C-terminal Gly.
source: In this pathway, UFM1 is first proteolytically processed by a UFM1-specific peptidase 1/2 (UFSP1/2) to expose a C-terminal Gly (Kang et al., 2007; Komatsu et al., 2004; Millrine et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kang et al., 2007; Komatsu et al., 2004; Millrine et al., 2022.

claim: UBA5 activates UFM1 through ATP-dependent adenylation of the UFM1 C-terminal Gly.
source: UBA5 activates UFM1 through ATP-dependent adenylation of the UFM1 C-terminal Gly, which is then transferred onto the UBA5 active site Cys 250, forming a high-energy thioester intermediate.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies (Gavin et al., 2014; Komatsu et al., 2004).

claim: The UFM1-specific E2 conjugating enzyme, UFC1, receives UFM1 from UBA5 onto its active site Cys through a transthiolation reaction.
source: Next, the UFM1-specific E2 conjugating enzyme, UFC1, binds to the activated UBA5–UFM1 intermediate and receives UFM1 onto its active site Cys through a transthiolation reaction (Figure 1A; Gavin et al., 2014; Komatsu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gavin et al., 2014; Komatsu et al., 2004 and Figure 1A.

claim: The UFM1 activation and transthiolation processes are achieved by a trans-binding mechanism involving two molecules each of UBA5, UFM1, and UFC1.
source: The UFM1 activation and transthiolation processes are achieved by a trans-binding mechanism involving two molecules each of UBA5, UFM1, and UFC1, wherein one UBA5 protomer performs the enzymatic processes while the other provides essential UFM1- and UFC1-binding sites in trans (Figure 1B; Kumar et al., 2021; Mashahreh et al., 2018; Oweis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kumar et al., 2021; Mashahreh et al., 2018; Oweis et al., 2016 and Figure 1B.

claim: The E3 ligase UFL1 functions as a scaffold to bring the activated UFC1–UFM1 conjugate to the substrate protein and facilitate the conjugation of UFM1 to a substrate Lys residue.
source: Next, the E3 ligase UFL1 functions as a scaffold to bring the activated UFC1–UFM1 conjugate to the substrate protein and facilitate the conjugation of UFM1 to a substrate Lys residue (Peter et al., 2022; Tatsumi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peter et al., 2022; Tatsumi et al., 2010.

claim: UFMylation has been implicated in regulating genome stability and receptor activation.
source: UFMylation has been implicated in regulating many processes such as genome stability and receptor activation (Liu et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Yoo et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Yoo et al., 2014.

claim: The principal role of UFMylation is believed to be in regulating proteotoxic stress at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: but the principal role is believed to be in regulating proteotoxic stress at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where UFMylation of stalled ribosomes initiates quality control measures (Liang et al., 2020; Scavone et al., 2023; Walczak et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liang et al., 2020; Scavone et al., 2023; Walczak et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020.

claim: A mouse model in which Uba5 is removed causes embryonic lethality due to hematopoietic defects.
source: So far, the only well-characterized Uba5 mutant animal model is a mouse model in which removal of the gene causes embryonic lethality due to hematopoietic defects (Tatsumi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tatsumi et al., 2011.

claim: Tissue-specific mouse knockouts of other genes within the UFMylation pathway support a role in regulating ER stress within secretory cells.
source: Tissue-specific mouse knockouts of other genes within the UFMylation pathway support a role in regulating ER stress within secretory cells, as well as a critical developmental role within the central nervous system (CNS) (Muona et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muona et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2019.

claim: 24 individuals from 17 families who have UBA5-associated DEE44 have been reported to date.
source: To date, 24 individuals from 17 families who have UBA5-associated DEE44 have been reported (Arnadottir et al., 2017; Briere et al., 2021; Colin et al., 2016; Daida et al., 2018; Low et al., 2019; Mignon-Ravix et al., 2018; Muona et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple clinical reports.

claim: Prior functional studies using cultured cells or patient cells show that many reported UBA5 variants cause various levels of loss of function (LoF).
source: Prior functional studies using cultured cells or patient cells show that many reported UBA5 variants cause various levels of loss of function (LoF).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by references to prior literature.

claim: The reported proband is a 3-year boy with axial hypotonia, generalized dystonia and lower extremity spasticity, global developmental delay, esotropia, and failure to thrive.
source: The reported proband is a 3-year boy with axial hypotonia, generalized dystonia and lower extremity spasticity, global developmental delay, esotropia, and failure to thrive.
evidence: This is a clinical observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: The proband had frequent vomiting with feeds and failure to thrive requiring gastrostomy tube placement in infancy.
source: In infancy he had frequent vomiting with feeds and failure to thrive requiring gastrostomy tube placement.
evidence: This is a clinical observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: At 4 months of age developmental delay and abnormal tone were noted in the proband.
source: At 4 months of age developmental delay and abnormal tone were noted.
evidence: This is a clinical observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: At 30 months of age, the proband rolls occasionally but does not sit, has a limited ability to grab objects, babbles, and follows familiar commands.
source: At 30 months of age, he rolls occasionally but does not sit, has a limited ability to grab objects, babbles, and follows familiar commands.
evidence: This is a clinical observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: An electroencephalogram at 7 months of age showed multifocal epileptiform discharges in drowsiness and sleep in the proband.
source: An electroencephalogram at 7 months of age showed multifocal epileptiform discharges in drowsiness and sleep.
evidence: This is a clinical observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: The proband has not had seizures.
source: He has not had seizures.
evidence: This is a clinical observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: The proband's MRI studies at 7 and 23 months of age show a slightly thin corpus callosum, posterior periventricular white matter T2 hyperintensity resulting in increased conspicuity of the subcortical U-fibers and widening of the Sylvian fissures.
source: His MRI studies at 7 and 23 months of age were read as normal, although on review show a slightly thin corpus callosum, posterior periventricular white matter T2 hyperintensity resulting in increased conspicuity of the subcortical U-fibers and widening of the Sylvian fissures (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is a clinical observation reported in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: The proband was found to have compound heterozygous variants in UBA5, NM_024818.6:c.169A>G (p.Met57Val) and c.935A>T (p.Gln312Leu) on trio exome sequencing.
source: On trio exome sequencing, the proband was found to have compound heterozygous variants in UBA5, NM_024818.6:c.169A>G (p.Met57Val) and c.935A>T (p.Gln312Leu).
evidence: This is genetic data obtained from clinical testing.

claim: The p.Met57Val variant was inherited from the proband's mother and the p.Gln312Leu variant was inherited from his father.
source: The p.Met57Val variant was inherited from his mother and the p.Gln312Leu variant was inherited from his father.
evidence: This is genetic data obtained from clinical testing.

claim: The p.Met57Val variant has been reported in one individual with DEE44.
source: The p.Met57Val variant has been reported in one individual with DEE44 (Colin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Colin et al., 2016.

claim: The p.Gln312Leu variant has not been previously reported.
source: The p.Gln312Leu variant has not been previously reported.
evidence: This is based on literature review.

claim: Neither the p.Met57Val nor p.Gln312Leu variant is reported in the gnomAD database v.2.1.1.
source: Neither variant is reported in the gnomAD database v.2.1.1 (https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org).
evidence: This is based on database query.

claim: Both p.Met57Val and p.Gln312Leu variants are predicted to be damaging or probably damaging by multiple pathogenicity prediction tools.
source: Both variants are predicted to be damaging or probably damaging by multiple pathogenicity prediction tools (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on computational predictions shown in Table 2.

claim: Uba5 is the ortholog of human UBA5 in flies.
source: Uba5 is the ortholog of human UBA5 in flies (UBA5 refers to the human gene; Uba5 refers to the fly gene).
evidence: This is based on orthology analysis.

claim: Human UBA5 and fly Uba5 proteins share 64% identity and 75% similarity in amino acid sequence.
source: The two proteins share 64% identity and 75% similarity in amino acid sequence, and the Drosophila Integrative Ortholog Prediction Tool (DIOPT) score between UBA5 and Uba5 is 15/16, indicating a high degree of homology (Figure 2A; Hu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 2A and cited from Hu et al., 2021.

claim: The DIOPT score between UBA5 and Uba5 is 15/16, indicating a high degree of homology.
source: The two proteins share 64% identity and 75% similarity in amino acid sequence, and the Drosophila Integrative Ortholog Prediction Tool (DIOPT) score between UBA5 and Uba5 is 15/16, indicating a high degree of homology (Figure 2A; Hu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on DIOPT analysis cited from Hu et al., 2021.

claim: The UBA5 protein has an adenylation domain, a UFM1-interacting sequence (UIS) and a UFC1-binding sequence (UBS), all of which are required for UFM1 activation and transthiolation.
source: The UBA5 protein has an adenylation domain, a UFM1-interacting sequence (UIS) and a UFC1-binding sequence (UBS), all of which are required for UFM1 activation and transthiolation (Bacik et al., 2010; Habisov et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2021; Padala et al., 2017; Xie, 2014; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Uba5 has all three highly conserved functional domains (adenylation domain, UIS, and UBS).
source: Similarly, Uba5 has all three highly conserved functional domains, and all of the amino acid residues affected by the DEE44-associated variants reported so far are conserved in the fly protein (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All of the amino acid residues affected by the DEE44-associated variants reported so far are conserved in the fly Uba5 protein.
source: Similarly, Uba5 has all three highly conserved functional domains, and all of the amino acid residues affected by the DEE44-associated variants reported so far are conserved in the fly protein (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Homozygous female and hemizygous male flies with the Uba5T2A-Gal4 allele are lethal at the embryonic stage.
source: For both alleles, homozygous female and hemizygous male flies are lethal at the embryonic stage, although a few Uba5T2A-Gal4 escapers survive to the L1 larval stage (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Homozygous female and hemizygous male flies with the Uba5KO allele are lethal at the embryonic stage.
source: For both alleles, homozygous female and hemizygous male flies are lethal at the embryonic stage, although a few Uba5T2A-Gal4 escapers survive to the L1 larval stage (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The lethality of Uba5T2A-Gal4 and Uba5KO flies is rescued by a genomic rescue (GR) construct that carries the Uba5 locus.
source: The lethality is rescued by a genomic rescue (GR) construct that carries the Uba5 locus (P[acman] clone CH321-02B13) (Venken et al., 2010), indicating that the lethality in both lines is caused by the LoF of Uba5.
evidence: This is experimental data showing genetic rescue.

claim: Expression of flippase (FLP) using Uba5T2A-Gal4 removes the insertion of the CRIMIC cassette and reverts the lethality of the Uba5T2A-Gal4 hemizygous males.
source: Moreover, expression of flippase (FLP) using Uba5T2A-Gal4 removes the insertion of the CRIMIC cassette and reverts the lethality of the Uba5T2A-Gal4 hemizygous males, showing that the lethality is indeed caused by the Uba5T2A-Gal4 allele (Figure 2D; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2D and cited from Lee et al., 2018.

claim: Expression of reference human UBA5 cDNA using Uba5T2A-Gal4 rescues the lethality of the mutants.
source: Finally, expression of reference human UBA5 cDNA using Uba5T2A-Gal4 rescues the lethality of the mutants, showing that the functions of the fly and human proteins are evolutionarily conserved (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The functions of the fly Uba5 and human UBA5 proteins are evolutionarily conserved.
source: Finally, expression of reference human UBA5 cDNA using Uba5T2A-Gal4 rescues the lethality of the mutants, showing that the functions of the fly and human proteins are evolutionarily conserved (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Uba5 is expressed in multiple tissues in L3 larvae and adult flies.
source: Uba5 is expressed in multiple tissues in L3 larvae and adult flies (Figure 3A), consistent with high-throughput gene expression profiling results (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Leader et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on expression analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, supported by citations to Leader et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022.

claim: In both larval CNS and adult brain, Uba5 is expressed in a subset of neurons and glia.
source: In both larval CNS and adult brain, the mCherry.nls signals are found in a subset of neurons and glia (Figure 3B, C), suggesting that Uba5 is expressed in the fly CNS but not in all cells.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Uba5 is expressed more widely in the adult brains than in the larval CNS.
source: Uba5 is expressed more widely in the adult brains than in the larval CNS.
evidence: This is based on comparison of expression patterns in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: In larval CNS, Uba5 is expressed in many fewer neurons than Elav.
source: In larval CNS, it is expressed in many fewer neurons than Elav (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The expression pattern of Uba5 resembles that of the para gene, which encodes the sole voltage-gated sodium channel in Drosophila that is only expressed in differentiated, actively firing neurons.
source: The expression pattern resembles that of the para gene, which encodes the sole voltage-gated sodium channel in Drosophila that is only expressed in differentiated, actively firing neurons (Ravenscroft et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison to known expression patterns cited from Ravenscroft et al., 2020.

claim: UBA5 may be required for the activity of neurons.
source: This suggests that UBA5 may be required for the activity of neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern similarity to para gene.

claim: Ubiquitous expression of UBA5 by da-Gal4 or Act-Gal4 fully rescues the lethality of the Uba5KO hemizygous mutant animals.
source: Ubiquitous expression of UBA5 by da-Gal4 or Act-Gal4 fully rescues the lethality of the mutant animals.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Tissue-specific expression of UBA5 in fat body (lpp-Gal4), muscles (Mef2-Gal4), neurons (Elav-Gal4), or glial cells (Repo-Gal4) fails to rescue the lethality of Uba5KO hemizygous mutants.
source: However, tissue-specific expression of UBA5 in fat body (lpp-Gal4), muscles (Mef2-Gal4), neurons (Elav-Gal4), or glial cells (Repo-Gal4) fails to rescue the lethality (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Uba5 is required in multiple tissues.
source: Hence, we conclude that Uba5 is required in multiple tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: Overexpression of UBA5 in Uba5KO/+ heterozygous flies does not cause any obvious phenotype.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of UBA5 in Uba5KO/+ heterozygous flies does not cause any obvious phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), showing that Uba5 overexpression is not overtly toxic.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Uba5 overexpression is not overtly toxic.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of UBA5 in Uba5KO/+ heterozygous flies does not cause any obvious phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), showing that Uba5 overexpression is not overtly toxic.
evidence: This is inferred from the overexpression experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A synthetic enzyme-dead UBA5 mutant p.Cys250Ala failed to rescue lethality at all temperatures tested (29, 25, and 18°C).
source: At all temperatures, a synthetic enzyme-dead UBA5 mutant p.Cys250Ala failed to rescue lethality (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Four DEE44-associated variants (p.Arg55His, p.Gly168Glu, p.Leu254Pro, and p.Cys303Arg) failed to rescue the lethality at all temperatures tested.
source: Similarly, four DEE44-associated variants (p.Arg55His, p.Gly168Glu, p.Leu254Pro, and p.Cys303Arg) failed to rescue the lethality at all temperatures tested, indicating that they are severe LoF.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Three variants (p.Tyr53Phe, p.Met57Val, and p.Val260Met) partially rescued the lethality at 18°C and the survival rate increased at elevated temperatures.
source: Three variants (p.Tyr53Phe, p.Met57Val, and p.Val260Met) partially rescued the lethality at 18°C and the survival rate increased at elevated temperatures (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The three variants p.Tyr53Phe, p.Met57Val, and p.Val260Met are likely hypomorphic alleles and support a dosage-sensitive effect of Uba5.
source: This suggests that the three variants are likely hypomorphic alleles and supports a dosage-sensitive effect of Uba5.
evidence: This is inferred from the temperature-dependent rescue data in Figure 4A.

claim: Six variants (p.Arg72Cys, p.Val260Met, p.Gln312Leu, p.Ala371Thr, p.Asp389Gly, and p.Asp389Tyr) fully rescued lethality.
source: However, six variants (p.Arg72Cys, p.Val260Met, p.Gln312Leu, p.Ala371Thr, p.Asp389Gly, and p.Asp389Tyr) fully rescued lethality, suggesting they are mild LoF or do not affect protein function.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The variants were stratified into three groups according to the activity of rescuing lethality: Group I (full rescue), Group II (partial rescue), Group III (failure to rescue).
source: Based on these results, we stratified the variants into three groups according to the activity of rescuing lethality: Group I, full rescue; Group II, partial rescue; Group III, failure to rescue (Table 3, Group I was further divided into IA and IB according to the other phenotypes described below).
evidence: This is a classification based on experimental data in Figure 4A and summarized in Table 3.

claim: The variants in Group II exhibited significant developmental delay as well as a shortened lifespan.
source: The variants in Group II exhibited significant developmental delay as well as a shortened lifespan, showing that they are partial LoF (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Some variants in Group I (Group 1A: p.Ala371Thr, p.Asp389Gly, and p.Asp389Tyr) caused neither developmental delay nor shortened lifespan.
source: In contrast, some variants in Group I (Group 1A: p.Ala371Thr, p.Asp389Gly, and p.Asp389Tyr) caused neither defect.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Other Group I variants (Group 1B: p.Arg72Cys and p.Gln312Leu) caused a shortened lifespan but did not affect the timing of development.
source: Other Group I variants (Group 1B: p.Arg72Cys and p.Gln312Leu) caused a shortened lifespan but did not affect the timing of development (Figure 4B, C), indicating that they are also partial LoF variants but could cause milder defects than Group II variants.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Flies with variants in Groups IB and II displayed reduced climbing activity at Day 7 and more severe defects by Day 30, showing a progressive worsening of the defects.
source: Flies with variants in Groups IB and II displayed reduced climbing activity at Day 7 and more severe defects by Day 30, showing a progressive worsening of the defects (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The variants in Group II exhibited a bang-sensitive phenotype by displaying seizure-like behavior and paralysis following mechanical stimulation.
source: Moreover, the variants in Group II exhibited a bang-sensitive phenotype by displaying seizure-like behavior and paralysis following mechanical stimulation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The Group IA variants displayed neither a climbing defect nor bang sensitivity.
source: However, the Group IA variants displayed neither a climbing defect nor bang sensitivity (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: The synaptic growth of fly larvae is not affected by the UBA5 variants.
source: Hence, we conclude that the synaptic growth of fly larvae is not affected by the UBA5 variants.
evidence: This is based on NMJ morphology analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Variants at positions Asp389 and Ala371 lie outside of the regions with determined structure.
source: Variants at positions Asp389 and Ala371 lie outside of the regions with determined structure, so their locations are modeled based on all available data.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: All Group IA variants localize in proximity of the UBS in protein sequence.
source: All Group IA variants localize in proximity of the UBS in protein sequence.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The p.Asp389Gly and p.Asp389Tyr variants affect Asp389 which is two amino acids upstream of the structurally resolved UBS.
source: The p.Asp389Gly and p.Asp389Tyr variants affect Asp389 which is two amino acids upstream of the structurally resolved UBS.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Previous biochemical and crosslinking data have demonstrated the proximity of Ala371 to the UFC1 active site.
source: For p.Ala371Thr, although there is no structure of this region, previous biochemical and crosslinking data have demonstrated its proximity to the UFC1 active site (Kumar et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2021.

claim: Four variants, p.Tyr53Phe, p.Arg55His, p.Met57Val, and p.Arg72Cys, affect residues near the ATP-binding site.
source: Four variants, p.Tyr53Phe, p.Arg55His, p.Met57Val, and p.Arg72Cys, affect residues near the ATP-binding site (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The side chain of Arg55 makes direct contacts to the bound ATP.
source: The side chain of Arg55 makes direct contacts to the bound ATP, while Met57 and Tyr53 make secondary contacts behind this site, and Arg72 makes more distant tertiary contacts.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Met57 and Tyr53 make secondary contacts behind the ATP-binding site.
source: The side chain of Arg55 makes direct contacts to the bound ATP, while Met57 and Tyr53 make secondary contacts behind this site, and Arg72 makes more distant tertiary contacts.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Arg72 makes more distant tertiary contacts to the ATP-binding site.
source: The side chain of Arg55 makes direct contacts to the bound ATP, while Met57 and Tyr53 make secondary contacts behind this site, and Arg72 makes more distant tertiary contacts.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Substitutions at positions Tyr53, Arg55, Met57, and Arg72 may affect the affinity of UBA5 toward ATP.
source: Substitutions at these positions, therefore, may affect the affinity of UBA5 toward ATP.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural proximity to ATP-binding site.

claim: Residue Leu254 is four amino acids downstream of the active site Cys250, contained within a loop region that must undergo conformational changes to support UFM1 activation and subsequent transthiolation.
source: Residue Leu254 is four amino acids downstream of the active site Cys250, contained within a loop region that must undergo conformational changes to support UFM1 activation and subsequent transthiolation (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The Pro substitution within the p.Leu254Pro variant may constrain the required flexibility of the Cys250 loop, thus impacting ATP binding, UFM1 activation, and UFM1 transthiolation.
source: The Pro substitution within the p.Leu254Pro variant may constrain the required flexibility of the Cys250 loop, thus impacting ATP binding, UFM1 activation, and UFM1 transthiolation.
evidence: This is inferred from structural knowledge about proline's effect on loop flexibility.

claim: Val260 is buried within the UBA5 homodimeric interface, opposing residue Val260 of the second protomer.
source: Val260 is buried within the UBA5 homodimeric interface, opposing residue Val260 of the second protomer (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The increased size of the p.Val260Met variant may cause a steric clash that reduces UBA5 dimerization.
source: The increased size of the p.Val260Met variant may cause a steric clash that reduces UBA5 dimerization, which would decrease ATP binding, UFM1 activation, and UFM1 transthiolation as a result.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis of the homodimeric interface.

claim: Positions Cys303 and Gly168 are fully buried, making structural contacts to support the fold of the adenylation domain.
source: Positions Cys303 and Gly168 are fully buried, making structural contacts to support the fold of the adenylation domain (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.
